clue.text: Cup brewed, chat freely to exchange latest news?

indicators.note: tea brewed in a cup is stirred about, so the word before it is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

indicators.note: used freely, without restraint, the word before it loses its fixed letter order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: Friends over a cuppa, chatting away and swapping all their news.
explanation.walkthrough: UPCATCH is an old word for 'catch up', and catching up with someone is trading the latest news; the question mark owns up to that stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch up with a friend is idiomatically to exchange recent gossip, and this rare verb is an old form of catch up.

clue.text: Verbal jokes, top to bottom, I had not noticed in Milton

indicators.note: in a down answer the top letter is the first, so it moves to the foot of the word

parts.note: puns are jokes made with words
I'd is the short form of I had

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they had missed the wordplay hidden in Milton's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Milton' marks the word as one poet's usage: Milton wrote UNSPIED to mean unseen.
explanation.definitionFit: Unspied is Milton's word for unseen or undetected, so something not noticed.

clue.text: Appoint world leader? Responsibility of No. 9

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to install someone in a post
third meaning: in rugby the scrum-half, wearing 9, feeds the ball into the scrum

explanation.surface: Who appoints a world leader, and is it the job of the man at No. 9?
explanation.walkthrough: No. 9 suggests a Downing Street address, but it is the rugby scrum-half's shirt number; the put-in is feeding the ball into the scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: To put in is to appoint; Vladimir Putin leads Russia; the put-in is the scrum-half's feed into a rugby scrum.

clue.text: Sandwich in container showing unexpected pigment

indicators.note: food in a tin or can is enclosed by it

parts.note: a can is a metal container
in the Caribbean a roti is flatbread wrapped round a curry filling

explanation.surface: A packed lunch in a tin turns out to be an odd colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpected' tempts as an anagram signal, but no anagram works; it belongs to the surface, the surprise of finding a sandwich in a can.
explanation.definitionFit: Carotin, usually carotene, is the orange plant pigment found in carrots.

clue.text: Baron buried in the rotunda fashioned in historical style

indicators.note: something buried in a place lies inside it
fashioned means shaped anew, so the letters are remade

parts.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for Baron

explanation.surface: A nobleman laid to rest in a round chamber built in a period style.
explanation.definitionFit: Tudorbethan is mock-Tudor architecture, imitating the Tudor and Elizabethan styles of the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Part of play (not amateur) including performance pieces moved slowly

indicators.note: including means holding within, so the next piece goes inside
not means without, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a play is divided into acts
A is the abbreviation for amateur
rep, short for repertoire, is the stock of pieces a company performs

explanation.surface: A professional theatre act whose performances dragged along slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: Crept is the past tense of creep, to move slowly and quietly.

clue.text: I'm Scot, tight — cause of regular amusement

indicators.note: tight means drunk, and a drunk's words come out in a jumbled order

parts.note: the six letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A tipsy Scotsman admits he is the regular source of everyone's laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' plays on the stereotype of the stingy Scot, but here it means drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A sitcom is a situation comedy, a television series that amuses viewers at regular weekly intervals.

clue.text: Pain when taken in by old dandy, artless crooked politician

indicators.note: something taken in by another is held inside it
less means minus, so that word comes out

parts.note: smart was once a noun for a fashionable man about town
the first three letters of this word, with 'less' as the signal to take them away
an ache is a dull pain

explanation.surface: A naive old fop, conned by a crooked politician, suffers for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'artless' looks like an adjective meaning naive, but it splits into art and less.
explanation.definitionFit: A sachem is a Native American chief, and in US slang a political boss, especially of Tammany Hall.

clue.text: Commanding disorderly private? I'm almost entirely restricting that

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so one piece holds the other
disorderly means out of order, so the letters are scrambled
almost means not quite all, so the last letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then jumbled
entirely means all of it

explanation.surface: An officer bawling orders at an unruly private, keeping him on a tight rein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' refers back to the jumbled private, which sits between the two other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperatival means of the imperative mood, the grammatical form used for giving orders.

clue.text: Pieceworker aunt employed casually, odd bits of time called in

indicators.note: something called in is brought inside
used casually, in a haphazard way, the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are the first, third and so on

parts.note: first and third letters

explanation.surface: An aunt hired as a casual pieceworker, called in for odd hours.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutman is a dialect word for a worker paid by the piece, from tut-work, piecework in mining.

clue.text: Reichenbach's theory, nothing depressingly avoided by ally

parts.note: O looks like zero

indicators.note: a word avoided by another is left out of it, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: a dismal mood is a depressed one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A friend shuns a scientist's theory, which came to nothing, sadly.
explanation.walkthrough: Baron von Reichenbach proposed 'od', a supposed natural force pervading all things.
explanation.definitionFit: Odism is belief in od, the vital force that the German chemist Karl von Reichenbach claimed to have discovered.

clue.text: He may be seen in Roman units (marching)

definitions.meaning: setter's reading: the Latin word for a foot soldier, who marches in Roman units such as legions, is spelt like the English plural for these distances
surface reading: distances in Roman measure, such as the thousand paces

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin for a soldier is spelt like the English plural of the Roman thousand-pace measure, so 'He' is a legionary on the march.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin the word for a soldier is miles, and a Roman soldier served in units such as cohorts and legions.

clue.text: Rough sound, one stirring in mud? That was river fish

parts.note: a burr is a rough rolled R or a whirring noise

indicators.note: something stirring in mud is churning it, so these words get mixed up

parts.note: A means one, as in a single thing
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A gurgling sound as something thrashes in the mud: was that a fish from the river?
explanation.walkthrough: 'That was' tells the solver this is an old spelling, now superseded by barramundi.
explanation.definitionFit: The barramundi is a large Australian food fish of rivers and estuaries; BURRAMUNDI is an obsolete spelling of its name.

clue.text: Pastry, its middle roughly left unfinished

indicators.note: a word left unfinished has lost its final letter
the middle of a word is its central letters, and 'its' points back to the first word

parts.note: 'its' points back to the first word, whose two central letters are kept
to treat someone roughly is to treat them rudely

explanation.surface: A pastry whose centre has been carelessly left half-baked.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition does double duty: 'its' refers back to Pastry, whose middle supplies the opening pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Strudel is a layered pastry, typically of thin dough rolled round a fruit filling such as apple.

clue.text: Ball entering landed back in net

indicators.note: going back means reading the word from its end to its start
one thing entering another goes inside it

parts.note: a bird that landed on a branch lit there
O is round, like a ball

explanation.surface: A tennis or football shot: the ball comes back down and ends up in the net.
explanation.walkthrough: TOIL in the sense of a trap survives mainly in the plural, 'caught in the toils'.
explanation.definitionFit: A toil is a snare or hunting net, the sense behind being caught in someone's toils.

clue.text: Power, one in progress as source of nuclear force

parts.note: P is the standard symbol for power
I is the Roman numeral one
a show that is on is in progress

explanation.surface: Power and progress hailed as the source of nuclear energy.
explanation.definitionFit: The pion is a meson whose exchange between nucleons carries the strong force binding atomic nuclei together.

clue.text: Item of underwear? Edge is visible in Church

indicators.note: something in a building is enclosed by its walls

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a hem is the edge of a piece of cloth
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's slip is showing in church, with its hem peeping out.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemise is a loose shift or slip worn under clothing, so an undergarment.

clue.text: Short piece of roofing timber? There's chopped tree in it

indicators.note: a tree chopped into pieces can be stacked in any order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A short roof timber: naturally there is a felled tree in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a container, tree inside it, but all three words go into the mix together.
explanation.definitionFit: An intertie is a short horizontal timber set between upright posts in a framed structure, such as a roof.

clue.text: Dry after exercise, tucked into pastry and liquid measure

indicators.note: a filling tucked into a pie is enclosed by its crust

parts.note: a pie is a pastry dish
PE is physical education
TT, teetotal, means not drinking alcohol

explanation.surface: After a workout, someone on the wagon tucks into a pie and measures a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipette is a slender glass tube used in laboratories to measure and transfer small amounts of liquid.

clue.text: Stamp collecting — it brought back glimpses of my boyhood somewhere in E. Europe

indicators.note: brought back means carried in the opposite direction, so read right to left

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a glimpse is only the first flash of something, so just initial letters

parts.note: the first letters of these two words
an Eastern European country

explanation.surface: Someone recalling how stamp collecting summoned memories of a childhood spent in Eastern Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Timbromania is an old name for philately, from French timbre, a postage stamp, plus mania, craze.

clue.text: Layout to do with strong hand makes this difficult

definitions.text: Layout to do with strong hand
definitions.meaning: surface reading: arranging something with a firm or forceful touch
setter's reading: a card bid to lose every trick, sometimes played with the hand laid out face up, is hard to make with strong cards

explanation.walkthrough: In whist and solo the bid to take no tricks can be played open, cards laid on the table; holding high cards makes losing every trick difficult.
explanation.definitionFit: Misère is a declaration in card games undertaking to win no tricks, so strong cards work against the bidder.

clue.text: Like Sandy's stubborn mount, no longer sluggish around race's end

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one piece goes about the other

parts.note: resty is an obsolete word for sluggish or restive

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of race

explanation.surface: A Scottish rider's horse, no longer lazy, balks at the end of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy is the crossword's stock Scotsman, signalling a Scots word; 'no longer' marks an obsolete one.
explanation.definitionFit: Reesty is Scots for restive or stubborn, used especially of a horse that refuses to go forward.

clue.text: Tricks of perverse girl, bird that's reverse of embarrassed within?

indicators.note: within means inside, so it sits in the middle of the other piece

parts.note: the jay is a bird of the crow family

indicators.note: the reverse of a word is that word read backwards

parts.note: an embarrassed face goes red

explanation.surface: A wilful girl playing tricks, a bird who is anything but embarrassed.
explanation.walkthrough: A jade is an old word for a headstrong or disreputable woman; bird is also slang for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Jadery means the wanton behaviour or tricks of a jade, a perverse or worthless woman.

clue.text: US grass snitches secretly in part

indicators.note: in part means only a section of the phrase is used

parts.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: An American informer quietly snitches on part of the gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' is British slang for an informer, which is why snitches fits the surface; here it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is an American name for a brome grass, a weed of grain fields also called cheat.

clue.text: What's confused with goral, emitting e.g. slow roar?

definitions.text: What's confused with goral, emitting e.g. slow roar?

indicators.note: confused means muddled, so what is left is rearranged
emitting means giving out, so those letters leave the phrase

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written and removed

explanation.surface: Which animal is mistaken for a goral and lets out a slow roar?
explanation.walkthrough: Whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the serow and goral are related Asian goat-antelopes, easily confused.
explanation.definitionFit: The serow is an Asian goat-antelope closely related to the goral and similar in appearance.

clue.text: Groundnut initially planted in the area that's wild

indicators.note: a seed in an area is set inside it
wild means unruly, so these letters run out of order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the first letter of planted

explanation.surface: A groundnut first planted in a patch of land that has gone wild.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthpea is a leguminous plant whose pods ripen underground, which is what a groundnut is.

clue.text: Bar — not a beautiful place for alcohol moderation

indicators.note: not means without, so that part is taken away

parts.note: temperance is moderation, especially in drinking
Tempe is a Greek valley famed for its beauty, and a byword for any lovely spot

explanation.surface: A pub that's no beauty spot: the temperance movement wouldn't approve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' tempts as the pub of the surface, but it is a plain bar of wood or iron.
explanation.definitionFit: A rance is a Scots word for a prop or bar, and also a red Belgian marble.

clue.text: Build what no complete rectory can be without

indicators.note: a phrase that cannot be without something must contain it

parts.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: Build what no proper vicarage should lack.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke reads as a building requirement, but it simply says the two words contain the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To erect a building is to construct or put it up.

clue.text: Smart thief, one likely to succeed pinching shimmering set

indicators.note: pinching something means gripping it between two sides

parts.note: an heir is due to succeed to a title or estate

indicators.note: something shimmering wavers and moves about, so these letters shift

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A crafty thief, an heir who can't resist pinching a glittering set of jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' is a nice double bluff: in the surface it means stealing, which suits a thief.
explanation.definitionFit: A heister is one who carries out a heist, a robbery, so a thief who works cleverly.

clue.text: Anorak needed in keener days

indicators.note: the letters sit in the next words, running across the gap between them

parts.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A warm coat would have been needed back when the weather was keener.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an anorak is a hooded weatherproof jacket, and by extension the obsessive enthusiast who wears one.
explanation.definitionFit: Anorak is British slang for a socially awkward obsessive with a niche hobby, which is a nerd.

clue.text: What may be seen in lectern emblematically?

definitions.text: What may be seen in lectern emblematically?

indicators.note: what is seen in a phrase is visible within it, spanning its words

parts.note: found across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A riddle about the emblem carved on a church lectern.
explanation.walkthrough: Church lecterns are traditionally carved as an eagle with spread wings, so the whole clue also describes the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, and an eagle is the emblem often carved on lecterns.

clue.text: I mixed vin, 50% TT, for guest rarely

definitions.note: 'rarely' marks the word as an uncommon one

indicators.note: mixed drinks are combined and stirred, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written
French for wine, taken as written
TT spelt out as two tees; half of it is one

explanation.surface: A host confesses to watering down the wine to half strength for a teetotal guest.
explanation.walkthrough: TT usually means teetotal, but here the letters are spelt out, tee tee, and half is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: An invitee is a person who has been invited, a guest; Azed marks the word as uncommon.

clue.text: Socialist with devious art I name endlessly anti-sophist?

parts.note: a standard abbreviation for Socialist

indicators.note: devious means taking a crooked route, so the letters go astray
endlessly means without its last letter

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled
to call someone something is to name them

explanation.surface: A cunning left-winger cast as a philosopher opposed to the sophists.
explanation.walkthrough: Socrates famously argued against the Sophists, who taught persuasion for fees; hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Socratical means relating to Socrates, the philosopher whose method was set against the Sophists' paid rhetoric.

clue.text: Equine muscular degeneration, very small in lateral duct

indicators.note: something in a channel lies inside it

parts.note: a sny is a side channel of a river, a North American word
wee is Scots for small

explanation.surface: A vet's note that a tiny blockage in a side duct has wasted a horse's muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeny is atrophy of the shoulder muscles in a horse, a wasting disorder of equine musculature.

clue.text: Gains yard, feeling very smooth

parts.note: velvet is old slang for winnings or profit
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A footballer gaining a yard, feeling silky smooth on the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gains' looks like a verb but is a plural noun; to be on velvet is to be in a winning position.
explanation.definitionFit: Velvety describes a texture as soft and smooth to the touch as velvet cloth.
